text.arabic_uthmani: أَمْ يَقُولُونَ ٱفْتَرَىٰهُ ۖ قُلْ إِنِ ٱفْتَرَيْتُهُۥ فَلَا تَمْلِكُونَ لِى مِنَ ٱللَّهِ شَيْـًٔا ۖ هُوَ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا تُفِيضُونَ فِيهِ ۖ كَفَىٰ بِهِۦ شَهِيدًۢا بَيْنِى وَبَيْنَكُمْ ۖ وَهُوَ ٱلْغَفُورُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ

words.gloss_range: disconnected rhetorical pivot, not a neutral alternative
words.prose: {{ar:أَمْ}} ({{tr:am}}) opens as disconnected challenge: the ayah pivots from the prior rejection (46:7) into the sharper claim of fabrication while already treating that claim as rhetorically suspect. Its first position launches the accusation-rebuttal architecture, moving from accusation to conditional concession, human powerlessness, divine knowledge, witness, and mercy. The clipped sound note is secondary, but it fits the abruptness of the pivot.

topics.headline: disconnected challenge particle
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the opening as an incredulous pivot into accusation, not as a neutral option in a list.
topics.reason: QAC identifies the particle as disconnected, and the local clause introduces the reported fabrication claim.

topics.headline: accusation-rebuttal launch
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the first particle sets the whole ayah into challenge mode before the accusation verb appears.
topics.reason: The following syntax supports a sequence from reported accusation through commanded reply, condition, knowledge, witness, and mercy.

topics.headline: prior-context escalation with acoustic color
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can register both the escalation from the previous accusation (46:7) and the abrupt oral feel of the opening.
topics.reason: The prior-context link is useful, while the phonetic observation remains supportive color rather than a controlling parse.

words.gloss_range: ongoing public saying of the accusation
words.root_gloss_range: saying, speaking, and articulated assertion; locally an imperfect third-plural report of opponent discourse

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: commanded saying that introduces the authorized reply

words.prose: {{ar:يَقُولُونَ}} ({{tr:yaqūlūna}}) casts the charge as ongoing public speech, not a completed private suspicion, continuing the speech-conflict from the prior report (46:7). The speech root is then answered by {{ar:قُلْ}} ({{tr:qul}}), so the ayah sets opponent assertion against commanded counter-speech. Its pairing with the fabrication root belongs to a recognizable accusation pattern (10:38; 11:13; 32:3), while the local quote exposes their own wording for rebuttal.

topics.headline: ongoing public accusation
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the accusation as a continuing discourse pattern rather than a one-time remark.
topics.reason: The imperfect third-plural verb governs the quoted claim and presents the opponents as ongoing speakers.

topics.headline: speech root becomes contested channel
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the same speech channel is occupied first by the opponents and then by the commanded answer.
topics.reason: The local q-w-l sequence moves from imperfect third plural to imperative singular.

topics.headline: saying plus fabrication formula
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the charge as part of a wider Quranic polemical pattern where saying and fabrication are paired (10:38; 11:13; 32:3).
topics.reason: The local phrase combines the speech verb with the Form VIII fabrication verb, matching the cited accusation contexts.

topics.headline: quoted accusation exposed
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the opponents' own formulation brought into the open before the reply begins.
topics.reason: The verb introduces a direct quoted charge and continues the speech-conflict from the previous context (46:7).

words.gloss_range: their quoted claim that he fabricated it
words.root_gloss_range: cutting, splitting, and derived fabrication; locally Form VIII false attribution with an attached object pronoun

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: if I fabricated it, the first-person conditional mirror of the accusation

words.prose: {{ar:ٱفْتَرَىٰهُ}} ({{tr:iftarāhu}}) gives the accusation as a perfect, completed claim from the opponents' viewpoint. The f-r-y background lets fabrication carry the image of cutting and reshaping truth, but the local Form VIII sense is false attribution, not literal cutting. The attached pronoun keeps the disputed revelation as the object, and the same verb will be mirrored in first person at {{ar:ٱفْتَرَيْتُهُۥ}} ({{tr:iftaraytuhu}}).

topics.headline: completed quoted accusation
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the rebuttal confront the accusation at full force as the opponents state it.
topics.reason: The perfect Form VIII verb stands inside the direct quotation governed by the speech verb.

topics.headline: cutting image behind false attribution
topics.reader_payoff: The reader senses fabrication as a violent reshaping of truth while keeping the actual local sense as forged attribution.
topics.reason: V4 supports the root's cutting and fabrication branches, but the local Form VIII verb selects the fabrication branch.

topics.headline: Form VIII with attached object
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices both the crafted-attribution form and the pronoun that keeps the disputed revelation constant.
topics.reason: QAC marks Form VIII with an attached object pronoun, and the same object pronoun recurs in the conditional echo.

topics.headline: accusation mirrored in the reply
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the opponent's wording become the raw material of the reply rather than being ignored.
topics.reason: The same root, form, and object relation recur at word 6 with a first-person subject.

words.gloss_range: commanded saying that introduces the authorized reply
words.root_gloss_range: speech and saying; locally a Form I imperative that turns reported accusation into commissioned response
words.prose: {{ar:قُلْ}} ({{tr:qul}}) reverses the speech channel: after what they keep saying, the Prophet is commanded to say the reply. The imperative makes him a relay for authorized counter-speech, not the composer of an unscripted defense. It also shifts the scene from narrated opponents (46:7) into direct confrontation, with the conditional reply extending to the mercy coda.

topics.headline: authorized counter-speech
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the answer as commanded speech that performs the rebuttal it introduces.
topics.reason: QAC marks a second-person imperative, and the attachment data makes it introduce the quoted reply.

topics.headline: same root reverses authority
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that opponent speech and commanded speech use the same root while authority changes sides.
topics.reason: Words 2 and 4 share q-w-l but differ in person, mood, and discourse authority.

topics.headline: hinge into conditional rebuttal
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the command as the hinge that turns accusation into a logical concession.
topics.reason: The command governs the long quoted reply beginning with the conditional particle.

topics.headline: narration becomes confrontation
topics.reader_payoff: The reader tracks the shift from talking about opponents to addressing them with an authorized argument.
topics.reason: The imperative mediates the transition from third-person report to second-person forms in the reply.

words.gloss_range: conditional particle introducing a hypothetical concession
words.prose: {{ar:إِنِ}} ({{tr:ini}}) turns the charge into a testable condition rather than an admission. The particle lets the reply grant the opponents' premise hypothetically, then send the consequence toward their lack of power before God.

topics.headline: hypothetical concession
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that the rebuttal does not panic-deny the charge; it tests even the strongest hypothetical version.
topics.reason: The particle introduces the protasis of the conditional sentence.

topics.headline: condition controls the answer
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the if-clause is designed to produce the apodosis of human powerlessness.
topics.reason: Attachment evidence links words 5-6 as protasis and words 7-13 as apodosis.

words.gloss_range: if I fabricated it, stated as a completed hypothetical with fixed object
words.root_gloss_range: cutting and fabrication; locally Form VIII false attribution repeated in first-person conditional form
words.prose: {{ar:ٱفْتَرَيْتُهُۥ}} ({{tr:iftaraytuhu}}) repeats the fabrication verb inside the condition but changes the speaker to first person. That shift lets the accused speaker voice the charge against himself, absorbing it as a premise and making it self-defeating. The suffixes keep both the hypothetical agent and the disputed object visible in one compact form.

topics.headline: completed hypothetical charge
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the condition test the charge as though fully completed for argument's sake.
topics.reason: The perfect verb stands in the conditional protasis.

topics.headline: self-reference absorbs the charge
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the rhetorical shock of the Prophet voicing the accusation in first person to strip it of control.
topics.reason: The 1cs subject marker shifts agency from the opponents' quotation into the commanded response.

topics.headline: same form with compact agent and object
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the same accusation preserved while person and argument structure are compressed in the verb.
topics.reason: Form VIII remains constant from word 3, while the 1cs subject and 3ms object are both morphologically visible.

topics.headline: repetition redirects the accusation
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that the same charge now yields the accusers' powerlessness rather than the Prophet's defeat.
topics.reason: The repeated f-r-y verb is embedded in the if-clause whose answer is the negated possession clause.

words.gloss_range: consequence marker introducing the conditional answer
words.prose: {{ar:فَ}} ({{tr:fa-}}) marks the answer to the condition. It does not let the granted premise land on prophetic guilt; it sends the logic immediately to the accusers' inability to possess anything for the Prophet against God.

topics.headline: conditional consequence marker
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the following negation as the necessary answer to the hypothetical premise.
topics.reason: QAC and attachment evidence identify the conjunction as introducing the apodosis.

topics.headline: premise redirected to accuser impotence
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that even the opponents' premise exposes their powerlessness, not the Prophet's vulnerability to them.
topics.reason: The particle links the if-clause to the negated possession clause.

words.gloss_range: factual negation of capacity, not prohibition
words.prose: {{ar:لَا}} ({{tr:lā}}) negates an indicative verb, so it states a fact of incapacity rather than issuing a prohibition. Coming immediately after the consequence marker, it blocks any expectation that the accusers can intervene, and the later indefinite object makes the denial total.

topics.headline: negated capacity statement
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees an objective denial of power, not an instruction to refrain.
topics.reason: The negation particle precedes an imperfect indicative possession verb.

topics.headline: consequence lands as denial
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the conditional answer close quickly on negation before the object expands it to nothing whatsoever.
topics.reason: The negation begins the apodosis clause directly after the consequence particle.

words.gloss_range: you possess or control, here negated as ongoing incapacity
words.root_gloss_range: possession, control, dominion, and kingship; locally a negated Form I imperfect denying control-rights
words.prose: {{ar:تَمْلِكُونَ}} ({{tr:tamlikūna}}) makes powerlessness the engine of the apodosis. Because the root ranges from ownership to dominion, the negation denies control-rights before God, not just practical ability. The phrase belongs to a recurring denial formula with God and thingness (5:17; 48:11), compressing human leverage to zero.

topics.headline: ongoing incapacity
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the denial as structural inability, not a temporary failed attempt.
topics.reason: The imperfect second-plural verb is negated by the preceding particle.

topics.headline: possession-root denies dominion
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the wording denies ownership and control, not merely the weaker idea of ability.
topics.reason: The m-l-k root supports possession, control, and sovereignty ranges, while local negation denies them in this clause.

topics.headline: no-leverage formula
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the clause as part of a Quranic formula denying human power before divine decree (5:17; 48:11).
topics.reason: The local collocation aligns the possession verb with the divine source phrase and the indefinite object.

topics.headline: structural center of the answer
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the verb organize the beneficiary phrase, divine source phrase, and object into one answer.
topics.reason: The verb governs the clause's main complements in the conditional answer.

words.gloss_range: for me or against me as the affected party
words.prose: {{ar:لِى}} ({{tr:lī}}) routes the denied possession toward the Prophet's case. The preposition can be heard as benefit or liability here, and either way the result is the same: the accusers cannot secure anything for him or impose anything against him from God's side.

topics.headline: speaker as affected party
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the negated power applied to the Prophet's case instead of floating abstractly.
topics.reason: QAC marks a lām plus first-person pronoun in the negated possession clause.

topics.headline: benefit and liability range
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that both favorable and adverse leverage are denied, while the local point remains lack of power before God.
topics.reason: The lām relation can support benefit or disadvantage, but both readings serve the local denial rather than creating two separate claims.

words.gloss_range: from or against God as decisive source
words.prose: {{ar:مِنَ}} ({{tr:mina}}) makes the denied leverage face the divine source. The preposition is not mere spatial separation here; with the following divine name, it frames the question as whether anyone can possess protection from or against God. That source-axis prepares the later witness formula.

topics.headline: source against which no leverage exists
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the issue shift from human argument to divine authority as the source no one can intercept.
topics.reason: QAC marks the preposition as governing the divine name and indicating the source against whom protection is sought.

topics.headline: prepares witness arbitration
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the clause begin moving from accusation into accountability before the later witness declaration.
topics.reason: The source phrase sits before the knowledge and witness clauses that complete the forensic frame.

words.gloss_range: the divine name governed by min, source of inescapable authority
words.root_gloss_range: proper divine name with worship/refuge associations; locally genitive after min and the pivot from human inability to divine knowledge

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: from or against God as decisive source

words.prose: {{ar:ٱللَّهِ}} ({{tr:allāhi}}) is genitive after {{ar:مِنَ}} ({{tr:mina}}), embedding divine authority as the source from which no human protection can be possessed. The divine name stands at the hinge: before it, the clause denies human leverage; after it, the ayah asserts divine knowledge. Its no-leverage setting also belongs to a mercy-as-argument thread that later offers forgiveness to responders (46:31). Derivational worship and refuge pressures may enrich the name, but the local grammar fixes it as the decisive divine referent.

topics.headline: genitive divine source
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees God grammatically installed as the source before whom the accusers' control fails.
topics.reason: QAC marks the divine name as genitive governed by the preceding preposition.

topics.headline: divine name with worship pressure
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can hear worship and refuge pressure behind the name while keeping the local point on absolute divine authority.
topics.reason: The derivational dispute is meaningful background, but the local surface is the proper divine name in a governed phrase.

topics.headline: divine name in no-leverage formula
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the name anchors the clause's denial of every unit of human leverage.
topics.reason: The divine name occurs between the negated possession verb and the indefinite object in the local formula.

topics.headline: pivot from inability to knowledge
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the ayah pass from what humans cannot control to what God knows.
topics.reason: The word closes the powerlessness clause just before the independent knowledge sentence begins.

words.gloss_range: anything whatsoever as the negated object
words.root_gloss_range: thingness, entity, and possible will-association; locally an indefinite accusative under negation universalizing the denial
words.prose: {{ar:شَيْـًٔا}} ({{tr:shayʾan}}) seals the apodosis with absolute zero: an indefinite accusative under negation means not anything whatsoever. Its thingness pressure turns the denial into no entity, unit, or willed leverage that could affect God's judgment. The medial hamza note supports the abruptness of that zero but does not change the grammar.

topics.headline: indefinite under negation
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the denial as nothing whatsoever, not merely lack of some specific resource.
topics.reason: QAC marks the noun as an indefinite accusative object functioning as universal quantifier under negation.

topics.headline: thingness sharpened by will pressure
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the denied object is no possible entity or act of will against God, while local grammar still selects ordinary thingness.
topics.reason: The possible will connection enriches the root field, but the local noun functions as the object 'thing'.

topics.headline: object seals the denial formula
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the conditional answer end not on possession but on the object that reduces possession to zero.
topics.reason: The indefinite object completes the negated possession formula.

topics.headline: hamza reinforces abrupt zero
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can notice an acoustic hard stop matching the semantic closure of nothingness.
topics.reason: The phonetic point is compatible with the surface but remains secondary to the grammatical universalization.

words.gloss_range: independent divine subject pronoun
words.prose: {{ar:هُوَ}} ({{tr:huwa}}) re-centers the divine subject after the conditional answer. The new nominal sentence moves from what the accusers lack to what God knows, and its later repetition before the mercy attributes frames knowledge and mercy as parallel predications of the same referent.

topics.headline: divine subject re-centered
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the argument pivot from human lack to God's own subject position.
topics.reason: QAC marks an independent pronoun as subject of the nominal sentence.

topics.headline: pronoun frame for knowledge and mercy
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the repeated pronoun tying the knowledge clause to the final mercy clause.
topics.reason: The independent pronoun recurs at word 27 before the closing predicates.

words.gloss_range: better or best knowing, locally divine superior knowledge of their discourse
words.root_gloss_range: knowing, learning, teaching, and informing; locally elative knowledge predicate, not teaching or informing
words.prose: {{ar:أَعْلَمُ}} ({{tr:aʿlamu}}) is the predicate of the explicit divine pronoun, asserting superior knowledge as a standing nominal fact. The following prepositional phrase specifies the content: what they pour forth in the matter. The root family includes teaching and informing, but the local elative selects unmatched knowing as the answer to public accusation and prepares the later move from internal awareness to external attestation.

topics.headline: standing superior knowledge
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees divine knowledge asserted as stable authority, not as a temporary reaction.
topics.reason: QAC marks an elative adjective as predicate of the nominal sentence.

topics.headline: knowledge directed to their overflow
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that God's superior knowledge is aimed at the accusers' discourse, not left generic.
topics.reason: The predicate is followed by the bi-mā complement containing the overflow clause.

topics.headline: knowing rather than teaching
topics.reader_payoff: The reader keeps the root's cognitive range in view while recognizing that the local role is superior knowing.
topics.reason: The root has several cognition-related branches, but the local elative adjective selects the knower role.

topics.headline: knowledge prepares witness
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees divine knowledge become the basis for later testimony rather than a detached attribute.
topics.reason: The knowledge nominal clause precedes the sufficiency-as-witness clause.

words.gloss_range: content-linking preposition for divine knowledge

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: better or best knowing as the divine knowledge predicate
relative or nominalizing content of knowledge

words.prose: {{ar:بِ}} ({{tr:bi-}}) keeps the knowledge claim from floating as a generic attribute. It attaches {{ar:أَعْلَمُ}} ({{tr:aʿlamu}}) to the following {{ar:مَا}} ({{tr:mā}}) clause, making the accusers' overflow the specific domain of divine knowledge.

topics.headline: knowledge attached to content
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees exactly what divine knowledge concerns: the discourse they are flooding into.
topics.reason: QAC identifies the preposition as introducing the object or content of knowledge.

topics.headline: route into overflow clause
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the small preposition structurally routes divine knowledge into the following overflow verb.
topics.reason: The prepositional phrase mediates between the knowledge predicate and the relative clause.

words.gloss_range: relative or nominalizing content of knowledge
words.prose: {{ar:مَا}} ({{tr:mā}}) compresses the following overflow clause into the object of knowledge. Read relatively, it is what they pour forth; read nominally, it is their act of pouring forth. Both are useful because the ayah makes God know both the content and the performance of the accusation.

topics.headline: clause compressed into object
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees an entire discourse-flood folded into one compact object of divine knowledge.
topics.reason: QAC marks the particle as a relative pronoun introducing the clause that specifies what God knows.

topics.headline: content and act readings
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can hold both the content of their speech and the act of flooding it under divine knowledge.
topics.reason: The surface supports relative construal locally; the maṣdariyya reading remains a useful narrowing of what the knowledge covers.

words.gloss_range: you pour forth or plunge into discourse, locally with fīhi
words.root_gloss_range: overflow of water, abundant discourse, and extended outpouring; locally Form IV second-plural excessive discourse under divine knowledge

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: in it or concerning it, the discourse-space of the overflow

words.prose: {{ar:تُفِيضُونَ}} ({{tr:tufīḍūna}}) is the ayah's vivid speech-flood verb. With {{ar:فِيهِ}} ({{tr:fīhi}}), it means they plunge into or pour forth discourse concerning the matter, not merely speak once. The Form IV and second-plural imperfect make them active producers of excessive discourse; the water image, rumor-like circulation, and ironic outpouring color stay narrowed to that discourse sense. The rarity of f-y-ḍ makes the overflow especially salient as the content God knows, and the breathy-to-emphatic sound texture supports the swelling image.

topics.headline: overflow into a topic
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees their speech as flooding into the disputed matter rather than as random talk.
topics.reason: The Form IV verb takes the following fīhi phrase in the local relative clause.

topics.headline: active generators of excess speech
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the accusers remain directly addressed as agents producing the discourse-flood.
topics.reason: QAC marks a second-person plural imperfect Form IV verb.

topics.headline: water overflow mapped to slanderous speech
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the accusation-talk as uncontrolled overflow while keeping the local sense in the discourse domain.
topics.reason: The root's physical overflow range is valid background, but the local verb with fī selects discourse overflow.

topics.headline: wide-spread discourse color
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can hear rumor-like circulation and ironic outpouring as color, without making non-surface derivatives govern the parse.
topics.reason: Non-surface derivative and later technical associations enrich the semantic field but do not replace the local Form IV discourse sense.

topics.headline: rare overflow made knowable
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that a marked overflow verb becomes the precise content of divine cognition.
topics.reason: The rare root occurs inside the bi-mā complement governed by the divine knowledge predicate.

topics.headline: audible swelling as support
topics.reader_payoff: The reader may hear the word's recitational texture support the image of swelling overflow.
topics.reason: The phonetic observation is compatible with the surface but remains secondary to valency and lexical sense.

words.gloss_range: in it or concerning it, the discourse-space of the overflow
words.prose: {{ar:فِيهِ}} ({{tr:fīhi}}) gives the overflow a location or topic: their speech is poured into the disputed revelation or accusation-space. The pronoun keeps that disputed object present without naming it again, and its reference can cover the text, the charge, and the discourse around it under God's knowledge.

topics.headline: topic space of overflow
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that the overflow is directed into a specific disputed matter, not left aimless.
topics.reason: The preposition plus pronoun attaches to the overflow verb as its topical/locative complement.

topics.headline: layered reference under knowledge
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can hold together the revelation, the accusation, and the surrounding discourse as the sphere God knows.
topics.reason: The closest local reference points to the revelation/dispute, while the broader clause permits discourse-content layering.

words.gloss_range: it suffices; locally God is sufficient as witness
words.root_gloss_range: sufficiency, adequacy, and being enough; locally Form I sufficiency in the kafā plus bi witness construction

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: by Him or with Him as emphatic sufficing agent

words.prose: {{ar:كَفَىٰ}} ({{tr:kafā}}) moves the argument from divine knowledge to verdictal adequacy: God is enough as witness. The construction with {{ar:بِهِۦ}} ({{tr:bihi}}) does not ask for supplemental proof controlled by the accusers. It belongs to a recurring divine-witness formula used for authentication (4:79; 4:166; 13:43; 17:96; 29:52).

topics.headline: sufficient witness construction
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees sufficiency concentrated in God as the party whose witness is enough.
topics.reason: The verb works with the following bāʾ pronoun in the standard sufficiency construction.

topics.headline: no supplemental validation needed
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the response rests on objective sufficiency, not on obtaining another human-controlled proof.
topics.reason: The local Form I verb states adequacy, not reflexive contentment or external assistance.

topics.headline: authentication formula
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the phrase as part of a known divine-witness formula in authentication contexts (4:79; 4:166; 13:43; 17:96; 29:52).
topics.reason: The k-f-y and sh-h-d pairing recurs in the cited cross-surah witness assertions.

topics.headline: knowledge lands as verdict
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the ayah move from what God knows to the sufficiency of God's testimony.
topics.reason: The sufficiency clause follows the divine knowledge sentence.

words.gloss_range: by Him or with Him as emphatic sufficing agent
words.prose: {{ar:بِهِۦ}} ({{tr:bihi}}) installs God inside the sufficiency formula as the one who is enough. Whether described as emphatic extra bāʾ or agency-marking bāʾ, the effect is the same locally: sufficiency is bound directly to the divine pronoun, making the arbiter unmistakable without repeating the name.

topics.headline: pronoun marks the sufficient agent
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the sufficiency formula tied directly to God even though the noun is not repeated.
topics.reason: QAC identifies the bāʾ plus pronoun as referring to God in the sufficiency construction.

topics.headline: extra and agency bāʾ both converge
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that alternate grammatical labels for the bāʾ strengthen the same sufficiency mechanism.
topics.reason: The grammar can be described as emphatic or transitive bāʾ, but neither reading changes the divine referent or the sufficiency claim.

topics.headline: arbiter inside the formula
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the forensic scene expand by placing the arbiter inside the witness formula.
topics.reason: The pronoun sits between the sufficiency verb and the witness specification.

words.gloss_range: as witness, specifying the mode of sufficiency
words.root_gloss_range: presence, seeing, testimony, and witnesshood; locally an accusative faʿīl role specifying sufficiency
words.prose: {{ar:شَهِيدًۢا}} ({{tr:shahīdan}}) specifies how God suffices: as witness, not merely as a generic authority. The root combines presence, seeing, and testimony, so the word moves from divine knowledge to attestation between the parties. Its faʿīl form gives witnesshood durable force and lets God's seeing stand as the attested standard while active witness remains local. The same root will later introduce a human witness in the surah (46:10), after divine testimony is established first; its accusative ending also pairs the denied object and sufficient witness as argument pivots.

topics.headline: sufficiency specified as witness
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the sufficiency claim narrowed to the precise role of witness.
topics.reason: QAC marks the noun as accusative tamyīz specifying the sufficiency construction.

topics.headline: presence plus testimony
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears witnesshood as direct access plus authority to attest, not detached observation.
topics.reason: The sh-h-d root range supports presence, seeing, and testimony, while the faʿīl form supports durable witness quality.

topics.headline: active and attested witness range
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can register that God's seeing is also the standard attested by the formula, while active witness remains the local sense.
topics.reason: The faʿīl pattern may carry active or passive nuance, but the local tamyīz role selects God as sufficient witness.

topics.headline: divine witness before human witness
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees divine testimony established before the later human witness appears in the same surah (46:10).
topics.reason: The word completes the kafā witness formula and shares the root with the later witness scene (46:10).

topics.headline: complete arbitration chain

words.prose: {{ar:بَيْنِى}} ({{tr:baynī}}) marks the speaker's side of the witness interval. Because b-y-n links separation with clarity, the space between parties is not empty distance but the juridical interval where truth is made distinct. That clarity field answers the prior manifest-claim setting (46:7) and points toward later manifest language (46:32). Its construct suffix anchors one side before the repeated {{ar:بَيْنَكُمْ}} ({{tr:baynakum}}) supplies the plural counterpart.

topics.headline: speaker-side interval
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the Prophet's side explicitly marked before the plural addressee side appears.
topics.reason: QAC marks a relational noun in construct with a first-person suffix.

topics.headline: between-space becomes clarity-space
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the gap between parties becomes the place where witness makes truth distinct.
topics.reason: The root field supports between-ness and clarity, and the local witness clause gives that interval forensic force.

topics.headline: repeated between-frame
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees two sides of the dispute spatialized with God's witness over the interval.
topics.reason: The phrase repeats the relational noun rather than using a single shared between expression.

topics.headline: clarity thread enters arbitration
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the clarity field from the prior context (46:7) become juridical separation here and point toward later manifest language (46:32).
topics.reason: The cited same-surah b-y-n contexts support a local movement from clarity language into witness arbitration.

words.gloss_range: coordination between the two between phrases
words.prose: {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa-}}) coordinates the two {{tr:bayn}} phrases while preserving their difference. It keeps the singular speaker side and plural addressee side paired within one witness span instead of collapsing them into a vague interpersonal contrast.

topics.headline: coordinates the two sides

topics.reason: QAC marks the conjunction as coordinating word 23 with word 25.

topics.headline: link without erasure

topics.reason: The conjunction links two separate relational expressions with different suffixes.

words.prose: {{ar:بَيْنَكُمْ}} ({{tr:baynakum}}) gives the accusers their collective side of the interval. The plural suffix contrasts with the singular suffix in {{ar:بَيْنِى}} ({{tr:baynī}}), making one messenger face a collective audience. Repeating the relational noun spatializes the dispute as a measured courtroom-like gap, with witnesshood occupying the interval; the clarity pressure is no longer their asserted manifest claim but the judged space where divine witness distinguishes the parties.

topics.headline: plural side of the interval

topics.headline: one speaker against many

topics.headline: doubled between creates courtroom interval

topics.reason: The repeated b-y-n phrases and the witness noun jointly construct the spatial-legal frame.

topics.headline: manifest claim becomes judged interval

topics.reason: The local repetition echoes the prior between phrase and interacts with the broader b-y-n clarity field.

words.gloss_range: resumptive or circumstantial conjunction before the mercy coda
words.prose: {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa-}}) carries the ayah from forensic witness into the mercy coda. It can be read resumptively, introducing a fresh declaration, or circumstantially, showing God witnessing while being forgiving and merciful. Either way, the conjunction prevents the witness clause from ending as a merely punitive verdict.

topics.headline: resumption and circumstance both live

topics.reason: QAC allows the conjunction before the final nominal sentence to be resumptive or circumstantial.

topics.headline: witness turns toward mercy

topics.reason: The conjunction introduces the final nominal sentence after the witness clause.

topics.headline: argument moves beyond charge
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees mercy enter as part of the ayah's argument after accusation, not as an unrelated formula.
topics.reason: The final conjunction links the witness frame directly to the mercy attributes.

words.gloss_range: second independent divine subject pronoun
words.prose: {{ar:هُوَ}} ({{tr:huwa}}) reintroduces the same divine subject before the closing attributes. Its repetition with the earlier {{ar:هُوَ}} ({{tr:huwa}}) binds divine knowledge and divine mercy as parallel assertions about one referent: the One who knows and witnesses is the One who forgives and shows mercy.

topics.headline: same subject retained
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the mercy attributes kept attached to the same God who knew and witnessed.
topics.reason: QAC marks an independent pronoun as the subject of the final nominal sentence.

topics.headline: knowledge and mercy frame
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices a grammatical refrain binding epistemic authority to merciful identity.
topics.reason: The pronoun repeats from word 14 at the two major divine predications.

words.gloss_range: the Forgiving, definite intensive predicate after witness
words.root_gloss_range: covering, concealing, pardoning, and forgiveness; locally definite faʿūl divine epithet in the mercy coda
words.prose: {{ar:ٱلْغَفُورُ}} ({{tr:al-ghafūru}}) brings forgiveness into an accusation scene where punishment might have been expected. The gh-f-r field frames forgiveness as covering and protective concealment of fault, a striking closure after God has just been named witness. Its definite title begins the familiar forgiveness-mercy dyad, specialized here so the One who sees all is also the One who covers faults. The same-surah thread anticipates forgiveness for responders (46:31), while the heavy guttural onset remains secondary sound color.

topics.headline: forgiveness displaces expected punishment
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the accusation answered with an opening toward forgiveness rather than a threat.
topics.reason: The epithet appears in the final coda after the witness arbitration clause.

topics.headline: covering fault as pardon
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears forgiveness as protective covering of fault, not mere erasure.
topics.reason: The gh-f-r root field supports covering and forgiveness, and the local epithet selects that divine title.

topics.headline: definite divine title in a dominant dyad
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices a stable divine title beginning a familiar forgiveness-mercy pair rather than an isolated quality.
topics.reason: QAC marks a definite nominative intensive predicate, and the collocation profile supports the gh-f-r plus r-ḥ-m pairing.

topics.headline: the witness also covers
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the paradox that the One who witnesses everything is also the One who covers and forgives.
topics.reason: The forgiveness epithet follows immediately after the divine witness clause and before the mercy epithet.

topics.headline: forgiveness thread with sound color
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can connect this forgiveness coda with the later invitation to forgiveness (46:31), while the guttural sound remains secondary color.
topics.reason: The same-surah forgiveness link is substantive; the phonetic observation supports tone but does not govern meaning.

words.gloss_range: the Merciful, definite final predicate
words.root_gloss_range: mercy, compassion, womb-like nurture, and protective care; locally definite faʿīl divine epithet completing the coda
words.prose: {{ar:ٱلرَّحِيمُ}} ({{tr:al-raḥīmu}}) gives mercy the final word of the ayah. As a definite nominative predicate, it states stable divine identity, and the r-ḥ-m field frames that mercy as protective, nurturing care rather than bare legal pardon. It completes the forgiveness-mercy pair and turns an ayah that began with fabrication accusation toward compassion as its closing frame. The local mercy thread also reaches back to 46:12, while the final long īm/mīm landing and sun-letter fusion remain recitational color.

topics.headline: definite predicate of mercy
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees mercy asserted as stable divine identity, not as a passing act.
topics.reason: QAC marks the word as a definite nominative predicate in the final nominal sentence.

topics.headline: mercy as final evaluative note
topics.reader_payoff: The reader experiences the ayah's last word as compassion rather than threat.
topics.reason: The mercy epithet is the final word after accusation, condition, knowledge, and witness.

topics.headline: protective nurturing mercy
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears mercy as protective and nurturing care, while the local title remains the divine epithet of mercy.
topics.reason: The r-ḥ-m root field supports womb-related mercy pressure, but the local surface is the divine epithet.

topics.headline: completion of the dominant mercy dyad
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees mercy complete the forgiveness pair, making the coda a linked mechanism rather than two isolated attributes.
topics.reason: The r-ḥ-m root is paired locally with the preceding gh-f-r epithet and strongly in the co-occurrence evidence.

topics.headline: outer arc from accusation to mercy
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the ayah's outer movement from fabrication charge to divine mercy as the final interpretive frame.
topics.reason: The opening fabrication charge dominates the first movement, while the final paired mercy attributes dominate the close.

topics.headline: surah mercy thread with closing sound
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can connect the final mercy word with the surah's later mercy language (46:12), while its closing sound remains supportive color.
topics.reason: The same-surah mercy link is substantive; the phonetic observation is secondary to the lexical and structural closure.

topics.headline: assimilated title landing
topics.reader_payoff: The reader may notice the recitational fusion of the definite title as part of the smooth final landing.
topics.reason: The assimilation is a valid surface feature, but it remains recitational support rather than a separate interpretive driver.
